item.title: Total cultural victory (again)
item.description: We’re all progressives until the next election
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument: our verdict on the news, plus our writers’ key takeaways and everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict by Jerusalem Demsas

The Democrats’ overwhelming midterm victory seems to have ended what I like to call the interwoke period.

After two years of corporations, universities, and other cultural institutions racing to distance themselves from DEI, as well as tech CEOs falling all over themselves to glaze Donald Trump — remember the gold plaque?? — the desperate turn many of these same actors are now making to the left is pretty funny.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp went viral this week for calling himself, his company, or his worldview “progressive” eight times in the span of a 22-minute episode of Politico’s The Playbook Podcast. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet,” Karp proclaimed.

Methinks the lady doth protest too much.

Share

While it’s technically true that Karp has been calling himself a progressive since at least 2018, he’s clearly an adherent to the words-don’t-mean-things school of thought. I do not know Karp, nor have I ever spoken to him, so what is in his heart is unknowable to me. But I do not personally find it progressive to build ICE software that helps agents find and arrest immigrants as part of a brutal, unpopular, and un-American deportation policy supported by a negligible number of left-leaning voters.

Plus, Karp’s donation history makes very clear the bet he made on right-wing politics: He donated $360,000 to a Biden-Harris fundraising committee in 2023 before donating $1 million to MAGA Inc. the following year. Now that Democrats are set to control Congress, he’s eager to explain that all of Palantir’s products serve their interests: “I absolutely believe Palantir — all of our products are essentially progressive,” Karp told Playbook.

Karp’s blatant opportunism at least has the virtue of self-awareness. At one point in the interview, when pressed about his giving to MAGA Inc., he exclaimed that he’s not “the village idiot”: “Of course I give to everybody — what, you expect me to be stupid? — like, that’s just how I roll.”

Karp wants you to know that he’s in on the gag. I see that same self-awareness in progressives joking about people putting pronouns back in their bios and email signatures, turning data centers into Criterion closets, and converting the Trump ballroom into a COVID-conscious lesbian bar.

What’s interesting about these jokes is that nobody seems to believe that they’ve actually won the culture wars. The joke is that the people who abandoned progressive cultural signifiers the second they became politically inconvenient will be back performing them as soon as the incentives shift. An election can change how people act — and who they genuflect to — without proving that anyone's mind has actually been changed.

Subscribe now

After Trump’s reelection, the commentary treated his win as evidence that the culture itself had made a lasting shift right: toward bro-influencer politics and away from “woke feminization.”

By early 2026, The Washington Post was describing young Trump supporters who saw his victory as a “cultural realignment”; an Axios article about young Trump voters framed their opinions on masculinity and religion as a “sharp cultural turn” that could reshape politics for years.

But, according to early evidence, young men swung back toward Democrats in the 2026 midterms. Yet we have not seen any extended hullabaloo about how young men are obviously all cultural Marxists now. The coverage has been provisional; The Post questions whether men will stick with Democrats and quotes a researcher saying that young men were swing voters.

I don’t think this is a story about media bias in a particular political direction — after all, the 2016 Democratic primary also spawned a thousand takes about the rise of Bernie bros and the dirtbag left. The Guardian asked why there were “suddenly millions of socialists in America” and argued that Sanders hadn’t made young people socialists; he had just revealed them. And The Post reported that Sanders was “profoundly changing” how millennials thought about politics.

But the 2016 result didn’t mean that voters hated women, the 2024 result didn’t mean young men had become conservatives, and the 2026 result doesn’t mean the whole country is now ready to join the Democratic Socialists of America. The temptation to treat each big swing as a revelation of voters’ actual views is divorced from reality. An election might just reveal what voters are angry about, or what coalition they currently see as closer to their views, without proving that the country has permanently changed its mind.

I don’t know why everyone is drawing different lessons from 2026, but I know why I do: Since 2016, I’ve become intimately familiar with the concept of no permanent victories.

Winning an election can make a set of ideas feel dominant or inevitable — the long arc of history is bending my way! — and losing one can make your cause feel dead — we live in hell — but neither feeling holds up in the long sweep of history.

Many progressives lived through Obama’s supposedly durable coalition, Trump’s first victory, the great “racial reckoning” of 2020, Biden’s election, the corporate DEI backlash, the return of a seemingly-more-popular-than-ever Trump — and now, the great repudiation of the Orange Man. Progressives and liberals know better than to take even this, the biggest partisan election victory in at least half a century, as a sign of things to come.

The “no permanent victories” idea was best articulated by T.S. Eliot in a 1927 essay in which he argued, “If we take the widest and wisest view of a Cause, there is no such thing as a Lost Cause because there is no such thing as a Gained Cause. We fight for lost causes because we know that our defeat and dismay may be the preface to our successors’ victory, though that victory itself will be temporary; we fight rather to keep something alive than in the expectation that anything will triumph.”

The right may now be learning this same lesson. It is facing a country it thought would cheer a cruel deportation policy and hostility to non-white immigrants and realizing that, actually, people mostly just want eggs and gas to be cheaper.

And the left, I think, is embracing irony in victory because it knows the Karps of the world are not on its side forever, and that the people reaching for progressive language may not truly share the same commitments.

The Road to 2028 with Lakshya Jain

Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, gives us his update on the race to become the first president of the post-Trump era:

Everyone seems to have agreed that cost of living is the No. 1 issue for swing voters. But what I think pundits are missing is that it’s also the top issue for Democrats: In our polling, 62% of Kamala Harris voters graded this as a top-two concern. This is, after all, what catapulted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to his win over more well-known candidates.

But I don’t know that any of the Democrats trying to run for president have really shown an ability to engage with productive solutions on this issue that they can sell to a Democratic primary audience just yet. The primary winner won’t be the candidate who can outflank everyone else on Palestine, but rather the candidate who most effectively channels economic discontent.

My guess is that Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff could do it. But if he falls short, I would think the next most likely candidate is Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Neither former Vice President Kamala Harris nor Gov. Gavin Newsom has shown any inclination or past history of being able to recognize this problem, and I don’t expect them to start now.

On the Republican side, it’s still Vice President JD Vance’s race to lose. You might think that's because Vance is trying to put a bit of early distance between himself and the fantastically unpopular Iran War. But really it’s because no other Republican wants to run in this environment; even Secretary of State Marco Rubio has signaled he has no interest. The chorus calling for him to throw his hat in the ring will only grow louder, though.

Life of the Mind with Kelsey Piper

Kelsey Piper, The Argument’s staff writer reporting on AI, tech, science, education, and politics, tells us what she’s seeing in the world this week:

As my colleague Jeremiah Johnson summarized yesterday, Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia CEO came after revelations that the company interfered with a Department of Commerce investigation into export control violations by a related company. That company was controlled by a woman with whom Huang was having an affair, and one that was suspected of routing Nvidia’s advanced AI chips into China.

An intelligence community memo leaked to The New York Times argued that Huang’s paramour had ties to China’s spy agency. The lurid affair-related details are new, but concerns that Nvidia flouted export controls have been around for a while: At a $1-million-per-head dinner at Mar-a-Lago, Huang pressed President Trump to allow more chip sales to China.

I don’t know if the export controls are good policy or not. But having them and not enforcing them got us the worst of both worlds: infuriating China without actually securing leverage for a bilateral agreement to not chase dangerous superintelligence. Hopefully the policy that comes out of this shock will be better.

🌟Abundance Win of the Week🌟

Maibritt Henkel, one of The Argument’s writing fellows, gives us her pick for this week’s biggest win in the wide world of abundance:

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) cleared a key procedural vote in the Senate on Monday, the first of many legislative hurdles. If passed, the bill promises to significantly speed up the review process for major infrastructure projects, ease the build-out of high-voltage transmission lines, and ensure that technology companies shoulder data-center-related spikes in grid infrastructure costs.

But while BAAJA would likely streamline the construction of wind and solar energy projects, it would do so partly by limiting the power of outside parties to sue to block projects, angering some environmental groups and tribal leaders. While 73 senators voted to advance the legislation — prominent holdouts included Sen. Bernie Sanders and Sen. Jeff Merkley — BAAJA’s passage is far from assured in a closely divided House of Representatives where majority control is soon to change hands.

On Tuesday, the Congressional Progressive Caucus announced its official opposition “unless significant improvements are made.” A final Senate vote could happen as early as next week.

Top stories this week by Maibritt Henkel

Texas has been governed by a Republican trifecta since the 2003. Now that Democrats have finally broken it, they have to decide which policies of the ancien régime to keep and which to discard. Staff writer Kelsey Piper argues that, when it comes to education policy, there is much Texas Dems can learn from their conservative predecessors — even as they roll back excesses like the state’s expansive voucher program. School choice and rigorous curricula should be part of the liberal playbook, even if it means conceding that outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott was right about some things.

Both progressive and moderate Democrats won upset victories in the midterms. This has given rise to a heated debate about which types of candidates the party should run moving forward. Our director of political data, Lakshya Jain, developed Split Ticket’s Wins Above Replacement (WAR) metric for candidates, which is uniquely well-suited to evaluating this question. He finds that the moderation advantage, while real, was much smaller in 2026 than it used to be.

In The Argument’s irregular Mad Libs debate column, I invited Elizabeth Grace Matthew, a sex-realist feminist and author of the Substack Restoring American Adulthood, to debate whether feminism ought to define womanhood in terms of biological sex. Her argument is that institutions can protect and accommodate women only when they’re organized around the sex binary. My view is that this position only holds if you believe the most salient fact of women’s lives is their reproductive biology.

Worth watching…

On this week’s podcast, Matt and Jerusalem discuss the battle to define the midterms. Paid subscribers can watch or listen to the episode ad-free or read the transcript. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube or listen at their podcast provider of choice.

item.title: Say goodbye to anonymous posting
item.description: In April, I warned that I could identify people by the way they write. A new study suggests I was right.
item.content:encoded:
By Kelsey Piper

Welcome to The Closing Argument: our verdict on the news, plus our writers’ key takeaways and everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict by Kelsey Piper

This spring, I discovered that AI had destroyed my ability to write anonymously. No matter what steps I took to eliminate any sign of my authorship besides the text itself, Claude could tell it was me — even when the text was an unpublished draft on a topic I never write about, or my college application essay from 15 years ago.

I warned that the death of anonymity would soon come for the rest of the internet. Some readers of The Argument were skeptical: Was I sure I wasn’t leaking information to Claude when I posed the question? Anyway, most people don’t have millions of words of their writing on the internet, so they would be safe, right?

A preprint of a research paper released this week looks much more systematically at this phenomenon. University of Maryland researchers tested whether modern AI models could identify an anonymous peer reviewer using the authors’ own submitted peer reviews and those of Ph.D. students in some of the authors’ lab.

The researchers found that “Claude Fable 5.2 names the reviewer of 56% of 398 private peer reviews whose authorship was never made public.” (Expanded research looking at thousands more private peer reviews is forthcoming.) That’s one way of testing this phenomenon at scale, and it points to deanonymizing skills that are substantial even with people who are not particularly famous.

The paper used another approach as well: The researchers took comments made by active Reddit users after the model’s release date and asked the model who had written them; it got the username right in 69% of cases in the group with the most active posters. They tried stories written by well-known authors (those with over 1 million Goodreads ratings): it guessed those every single time. They tried papers posted to the scientific paper repository arXiv: The model was 46% accurate.

While these findings support my hypothesis that we’re witnessing a total erosion of the ability to write anonymously online, they also show that the process is still incomplete. Not everyone should consider themselves deanonymized yet. But the erosion is happening: My experiments in the spring convinced me that no prolific public writer could ever write anonymously again, and now we know that academics and even active Redditors should probably assume the same.

If you’re in doubt, there are ways to tell: The authors found that when they asked a model how well it knows an individual, it could correctly predict whether it could deanonymize them. So you can determine if you are vulnerable by asking a model how familiar it is with your name and any usernames you go by online.

What does this all mean? Well, for one thing, the institution of anonymous peer review does not look like it will hold up any longer. The space of possible reviewers for a given academic article review in a particular discipline is pretty small; stylistic tics are sufficient to confidently distinguish between them.

For another, the researchers find that today’s LLMs are also quite effective as a “poor man’s Pangram,” referring to the leading AI-writing detector — that is, they have similarly low false positive and false negative rates when asked whether the author of a text is human at all. (And, if the writing is done by a model from one of the leading U.S. AI companies, they can even name which company’s AI it is.)

While the Pangram haters are at it again in the aftermath of yet another controversy over whether to award literary prizes to obviously AI-written works, pretty soon every AI will be capable of identifying AI-written text with high accuracy. It’s part and parcel of their general abilities to identify text authors with high accuracy.

As for what a person can do if they don’t want to be deanonymized, it would be nice to have better answers. I am particularly concerned for anyone who writes anonymously while living under a repressive government, as well as for anyone who has disclosed sensitive personal information in anonymous Reddit posts and the like.

The paper finds that there’s not much you can do. LLMs almost never refuse these tasks. Deleting your internet presence doesn’t remove it from the pretraining data that the model is using to determine authorship. And the researchers find that even paraphrasing a human author’s text with AI does not eliminate a model’s ability to deanonymize that author.

Realistically, I still think we should accept that the internet is no longer anonymous if you write at any significant length. Institutions that relied on anonymity will have to figure out how to function some other way. But if you’ve stayed out of the training weights so far, you can likely continue to do so — by just never writing anything on the public internet. The models very rarely identified anyone who they were barely familiar with — at least on default effort settings.

The Road to 2028 with Lakshya Jain

Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, gives us his update on the race to become the first president of the post-Trump era:

In building our Wins Above Replacement model, I’ve been struck by how many things it flags ahead of time that we just choose to ignore, because they break our priors. Take Annie Andrews. Most people looking at her Twitter feed might have written her off as a #Resist grifter, but Andrews overperformed by 4 points in her 2022 loss to Nancy Mace, showing that she could absolutely run a credible campaign. Meanwhile, Lindsey Graham had always been tagged as a weak incumbent, underperforming by an average of 6.5 points in his last two elections. So when Andrews flipped Graham’s South Carolina Senate seat, beating Graham’s deeply unqualified sister, it shouldn’t have been a huge surprise to anyone looking at WAR.

What does that mean for 2028? Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has underperformed in four straight elections, making her one of the weaker incumbents in Congress, while Jon Ossoff has turned in two very strong performances. JD Vance, meanwhile, was a weak candidate in Ohio, and even Marco Rubio never showed much signs of electoral strength. I wouldn’t be surprised if this carried over to the presidential election to some degree, the question is whether anyone will heed the warning signs before it’s too late.

Life of the Mind with Jerusalem Demsas

In this section, Kelsey, The Argument’s staff writer reporting on AI, tech, science, education, and politics, tells us what she’s seeing in the world this week. This week I’m taking over for her:

Smartphones have been extremely bad for me in particular but I’ve been torn on whether they’re more like alcohol (really bad for a small subset, but broadly fine as an occasional indulgence) or cigarettes (truly no one should ever smoke a cigarette).

But what I’ve never understood is why there’s so much debate over whether it’s good to send kids to schools with a TV in their pocket. This week, a new study found that students at schools that required them to put their phones in locked pouches saw gains in math and reading equivalent to one or two extra weeks of learning a year.

Two co-authors of an earlier smartphone study came away with two very different reactions: “encouraging” and “largely disappointing.”

I’m glad that there are social scientists who preregister their views and tell us when results surprise them. But as a non-economist merely observing reality, I have to say there’s probably no study in the world that could convince me that children and schools aren’t better off with the phones put away.

🌟Abundance Win of the Week🌟

Maibritt Henkel, one of The Argument’s writing fellows, gives us her pick for this week’s biggest win in the wide world of abundance:

The Boston City Council voted to eliminate minimum parking requirements for new housing developments this week. If the proposal receives final approval from the Zoning Commission, developers will no longer have to provide parking when building new housing. It’s a small change on paper with big implications: Adding parking in Boston can cost up to $100,000 per underground space.

Eliminating parking minimums has already lowered housing construction costs in other cities. Seattle began ditching parking requirements back in 2012, and in the years that followed, developers built 40% fewer parking spaces, saving around $537 million. In 2023, Austin, Texas, became the largest city to ditch minimums and has since seen average rent drop by around 16.2%. The reform was just one of many that have contributed to Austin’s apartment-building boom, but it’s been cited as one of the key drivers.

In Boston, on the other hand, rent is up 2.5% from just a year ago. Given the entrenched NIMBY resistance to any and all housing reforms in Massachusetts — Question 7, a ballot measure that would have lowered minimum single-family lot sizes, was rejected by voters earlier this month — the City Council’s vote is encouraging.

Is the Bay State finally starting to see the light?

Subscribe now

Top stories this week by Maibritt Henkel

Why does it feel like there’s been a decades-long vibe shift against the ideal of progress? Staff writer Jeremiah Johnson traveled all the way to Berkeley, California, to find out. At Progress Conference 2026, he talked with policy experts trying to build high-speed rail faster, solar technology entrepreneurs, and philosophers trying to grapple with what humanity would look like if we ever conquered aging. All of them had different theories about why ideas like theirs can’t quite ignite the public imagination. One explanation, Jeremiah argues, is decades of inequality: A growing pie means nothing to local communities unless they believe that they, too, will get a slice.

Thursday was something of a Super Bowl for election data nerds, because The Argument director of political data Lakshya Jain released Split Ticket’s entire Wins Above Replacement (WAR) model for the 2026 midterms. Lakshya’s WAR scores compare the final result of every single two-party race to the expected result of a matchup between a generic Democratic and generic Republican candidates in the same district. As such, they’re good at revealing which candidates are truly exceptional and which just benefited from a good environment.

We know what types of disasters experts think AI could accelerate: cyberattacks, bioweapons, even human extinction. But what if we get staggering machine superintelligence without those massive downsides? Staff writer Kelsey Piper considers how a world without the need for human labor — or one where it becomes possible to marry your own mind to AI — would not actually settle the question of what makes a good life.

Worth watching…

On this week’s podcast, Matt and Jerusalem talk to certified Gen Z-whisperer Kyla Scanlon about why young people hate the economy. Paid subscribers can watch or listen to the episode ad-free or read the transcript. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube or listen at their podcast provider of choice.

Nick Bostrom, author of the 2014 book Superintelligence, and NYU philosophy professor Ned Block joined Kobe Yank-Jacobs for a Substack Live debate about AI consciousness.
